title: Where Is It?
description: Ask where something is with the Yemeni وين, answer with here, there, in, on and next to, and name the places a week takes you — the souq, the mosque, the school, the hospital — plus the two rooms every guest needs to find.
approach: GPA Phase 2 — a neighbourhood map and a house plan as the here-and-now; the learner asks وين and answers with فيه + place phrase, then locates objects from earlier lessons.
unlock_condition: ≥11/14 on the listen-and-tap quiz and three recorded وين questions with answers
can_do: Say here, there, in, on and next to
Name the places you go every week

grammar.title: وين؟ — where
grammar.explanation: Yemen's 'where' is وين. It can start the question — وين السوق؟ — or sit at the end, which is very Sanaa: السوق وين؟ Add an ending for a person: وينك؟ 'where are you?', وينه؟ 'where is he?'. Older Sanaa speakers keep the classical أين, and the south says فين; understand both, say وين. The answer usually starts with a place word: في السوق, هنا, جنب الجامع.

examples.english: Where are you? — I'm at home
Where is your mother? — In the kitchen

grammar.title: فيه / مابش + a place phrase
grammar.explanation: 'There is' in Yemen is فيه — literally 'in it' — and Sanaa also has its own به. Put a thing after it and then a place phrase: فيه شاهي في المطبخ 'there is tea in the kitchen'. To ask, raise your voice: فيه خبز؟ 'is there bread?'. For 'there isn't', Sanaa says مابش or ما فيش — the -sh on the end is the negation you first heard in ما فيش مشكلة. The place phrase can also come first: في السوق فيه خبز.

examples.english: There is tea in the kitchen
There is a mosque next to the house

culture.title: Ask anyone, and the mosque is the landmark
culture.note: Nobody in Yemen expects you to find your way alone. Stop a man in the street with اسمح لي، وين… and he will not just point — he may walk you there, and refusing his company is harder than accepting it. Directions are given by landmarks, not street names: the mosque, the bakery, the roundabout, the big tree. In Old Sanaa the walled city's gate باب اليمن and the Great Mosque الجامع الكبير anchor everything. You can walk into a souq, a shop or a courtyard freely; a mosque only if you are Muslim or invited, and a house only past the door where the host has led you — never further in, where the family's rooms are.

phrases.english: Excuse me, where is the Great Mosque?
Over there, next to the market

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Yemeni 'where' — shared with the Gulf, unlike the Egyptian فين which you will hear in the south. Takes endings: وينك، وينه، وينها. Old Sanaa keeps أين too.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man on a street corner with a map, looking around with raised eyebrows.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone asking for directions or hunting for an object; وين audible.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Sanaa says haana with a long first vowel — listen for it. The short هني is also heard. Point at the ground as you say it.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand pointing straight down at the ground at the speaker's own feet.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone patting a seat or pointing at their own spot; هنا / تعال هنا.

vocabulary.teaching_note: hunaak, with the stress on the long aa. Sanaa also says هوناك with an extra o. The word for 'over there' when you point across a street.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand pointing away across a lane toward a distant doorway.
vocabulary.video_hint: Directions given by pointing; هناك audible.

vocabulary.teaching_note: In, at, inside: في البيت 'at home', في السوق 'at the market'. Before الـ it runs together: fil-bayt. The same word with an ending gives فيه 'there is'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A key inside an open box, the box drawn large and simple.

example.english: My father is at the mosque

vocabulary.video_hint: Any location statement; في + place in narration.

vocabulary.teaching_note: On top of: على الكرسي, على الطاولة. Starts with ع. Also 'about' and 'against' later, but for now it is where a thing sits.
vocabulary.image_scene: A book lying on top of a chair, drawn large and simple.

example.english: The book is on the chair

vocabulary.video_hint: Objects placed on surfaces; على + noun.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'At the side of' — جنب الجامع 'next to the mosque'. Sanaa j, and some speakers say جمب. With an ending: جنبي 'next to me', جنبك.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two houses side by side with a small arrow between them.

example.english: The school is next to the mosque

vocabulary.teaching_note: The ق is a g: suug. Sanaa's old souq is سوق الملح, a maze of specialised lanes — the raisin souq, the silver souq, the qat souq. Where most of your Arabic will happen.
vocabulary.image_scene: A crowded covered market lane with sacks of spices and hanging lanterns.
vocabulary.video_hint: Souq footage; السوق named at the start of a shopping vlog.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The everyday word for a mosque in Yemen is جامع; مسجد is also understood. Ends in ع. The Great Mosque of Sanaa, الجامع الكبير, is among the oldest in the world.
vocabulary.image_scene: A white minaret with brown geometric bands rising above tower houses.

example.english: The mosque is next to the market

vocabulary.video_hint: A mosque as a landmark in directions or in Old Sanaa tours.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A feminine ة-word: المدرسة كبيرة. Same root as درس 'study'. Schools in Yemen run in morning and afternoon shifts, so children are in the street at odd hours.
vocabulary.image_scene: A school gate with children in uniform and backpacks streaming out.
vocabulary.video_hint: School gates and classrooms; المدرسة in family vlogs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Four syllables: mus-tash-fa. Every city has a big public one people name as a landmark — الثورة in Sanaa. Learn it before you need it.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hospital entrance with a red crescent sign and an ambulance parked outside.
vocabulary.video_hint: A hospital named as a landmark or destination.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Ends in ع. Big streets have names — شارع حدة, شارع الزبيري — small lanes in the old city do not, which is why directions go by landmark.
vocabulary.image_scene: A busy Sanaa street with shops, motorbikes and a minaret at the end.

example.english: The kids are in the street

vocabulary.video_hint: Street scenes; الشارع named or a street name given.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Doubled m and a ḥ at the start. The room you will need to ask for first in any house: وين الحمام؟ Also the traditional Sanaa bathhouse — حمام in the old city means the steam bath too.
vocabulary.image_scene: A simple bathroom door ajar showing a tap and a basin inside.
vocabulary.video_hint: House tours naming rooms; someone asking for the bathroom.

vocabulary.teaching_note: ط and خ in one word. In a tower house the kitchen is traditionally on a lower floor near the tannur oven; in a modern flat it is where guests are not usually taken.
vocabulary.image_scene: A small kitchen with a gas stove, a clay oven in the corner and pots on a shelf.

example.english: My mother is in the kitchen

vocabulary.video_hint: Cooking vlogs opening in the kitchen; المطبخ named in a house tour.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'There is / there are', and with rising voice 'is there?'. Sanaa's own version is به — بيه شاهي؟ 'is there tea?'. The negative is مابش or ما فيش, which the next lessons build on.
vocabulary.image_scene: An open fridge with bottles inside and a hand gesturing at them as if to say 'there is'.

example.english: There is bread in the kitchen

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone checking or announcing what is available; فيه / به audible.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.english: Excuse me, where is the market?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.english: The market is over there, next to the Great Mosque

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.english: And is there a hospital here?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.english: There isn't. The hospital is on Hadda Street

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.arabic: تعال معي، أنا في السوق كمان
dialogue.english: Come with me, I'm going to the market too

sound_spotlight.explanation: Two of the lesson's key words start with the Sanaa j. Say them against the Aden gaamiʿ, ganb and hear which side of the mountains you are on.
Sanaa stresses long syllables hard and squashes the rest. hunAAk, mustASHfa, madRAsa — find the heavy syllable first and the word will come out right.
The Sanaa 'there isn't' packs ما + به + ش into one word. The sharp -sh at the end is the negation marker, heard here before it is drilled in Lesson 11.

lesson_sequence.detail: A hand-drawn map of a Sanaa neighbourhood — souq, mosque, school, hospital, a street. One line of English: you will ask where things are and understand the answer.
Tap each place on the map to hear its name; then tap the rooms on a house plan (bathroom, kitchen).
وين، هنا، هناك، في، على، جنب، فيه as animated cards — an object moves in, on, next to; a hand points here and there.
Audio asks وين + object; tap the spot on the scene. Then the reverse: an object is highlighted; tap the correct phrase (في المطبخ / على الكرسي / جنب الباب).
All fourteen, audio only, four-image grid.
Record وين الحمام؟ وين السوق؟ فيه شاهي؟ and hear the model answers. Feedback on ج and ع.
Counter rolls up. Nudge: ask وين for three things you cannot see right now.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Say where five things in your home are right now: الكتاب على …، المفتاح في …، التلفون جنب … .
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen. Here-and-now location sentences with earlier vocabulary.

real_world_prompts.prompt: The next time you need a bathroom anywhere, rehearse وين الحمام لو سمحت؟ before you ask, even in English.
real_world_prompts.context: Follow-up notification. Anchors the highest-value question to a real need.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask your tutor to describe their neighbourhood using فيه and جنب, and draw the map as they talk.
real_world_prompts.context: Tutor prompt. Listening for location phrases with a physical output.
